# The Bottle

For thirty-one years, Elias kept the light at Cape Vesper, and for thirty-one years, the sea brought him nothing but driftwood and gull bones. He knew this because he had counted.

The morning it changed, the fog was thick as wool. Elias was polishing the lens when a glint of color caught his eye near the tide line—red, impossibly red, bobbing against the rocks. He waded out and pulled it in: a glass bottle, sealed with wax, its paper curling but legible.

*If you are reading this, the storm took me. I am off the coast of Cape Vesper, holding on to the wheel. The light is my only hope. — M.*

Elias read it twice, then a third time. The handwriting was cramped, desperate. He had no name, no date, only a position that matched the waters just beyond the reef.

He ran to the tower and swept the beam across the gray, watching it carve through the fog. Nothing. He adjusted the rotation, scanned the horizon, and for a long minute, the only sound was the wind hissing through the lantern room.

Then a shape emerged—small, dark, drifting close to shore where the currents would carry a wrecked boat. Elias fumbled with the radio, the thing crackling to life after years of silence.

"Vesper Light to any vessel in distress. Do you read?"

Static. Then, faint and broken: "Vesper... light..."
